name: Grace Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Grace, thanks for doing this. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union or party, and what you tell me stays confidential. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a trainee dozer operator at the Halden gold mine. Mostly I push waste rock on the dumps, shaping the slopes after the trucks tip. It sounds boring, but getting a clean batter, that's the sloped face, is harder than it looks. I do twelve-hour shifts, four on, four off.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the four days off, honestly, and I like being on my own in the cab with a podcast. What wears me out is being the new one. If a slope's wrong, the surveyor flags it on the tablet and everybody on the radio hears about it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a room in a shared house in town, near the pool. I'm single. I send my mum 150 a month because her hours got cut at the laundromat. So my savings are about three weeks, on a good month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's begin. The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, so mostly nothing. That's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, all that fuss. I'd maybe share a funny meme in the group chat. I don't really argue online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the same squeeze. Rent, my mum, and a trainee wage. The mine's fine for now, the gold price is good. But the gold mine is the only big employer within an hour, so if I lose this job there's nowhere close to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep getting better on the dozer so I can get my full ticket by mid-year, which is a pay rise. I'd try to build my savings up to two months. Maybe I'd use one of those AI budget apps my friend Jo uses, if she shows me how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tight. Normal tight. Not scared, just careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd cut if money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My weekend trips to the coast. I go every second break to see my mum. I'd hate to cut it, but I'd call more instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned an AI budget app. Do you use AI tools much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I asked one to explain my payslip once because the overtime looked wrong, and it was right. I don't go looking for new stuff, but if a friend's tried it, I'll try it.

say: I'd say **all that fuss** came to nothing.
I'd share a **meme** in the group chat but not argue online.
think: My **money squeeze** stays the same: rent, my mum and a trainee wage.
The mine is the **only big employer** within an hour, so losing it would hurt.
do: Get my **full dozer ticket** by mid-year for the pay rise.
Build savings to **two months**, maybe with Jo's AI budget app.
S0.quote: The gold mine is the only big employer within an hour, so if I lose this job there's nowhere close to go.
fieldNote: Grace's worry is **money and distance**, not AI: her mum's cut hours and few local jobs.
She tries new tech **once a friend has**, like Jo's budget app.
She'd cut **visits to her mum** before anything else, which shows how tight things are.

steps.text: Get the full dozer ticket by mid-year for the pay rise
Build savings to two months using Jo's AI budget app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one feels more like what's actually happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's changing, sure, but people will adjust. I'd probably say that to my mum on the phone, to calm her down. At work I'd keep it neutral, people get touchy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job's mostly hands-on, so it's slow for me. But the surveyors already use drones and software to plan the dumps. If AI does the planning, a remote dozer doesn't need a person in the cab for simple pushing. That's my job, the simple pushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my ticket first. Then I'd ask about moving onto the bigger dozers at the face, which need more skill and are harder to automate. Once a few people at the mine use the new planning apps, I'd learn them too. I'd keep sending Mum her money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can see a path, but it's not fully clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said simple pushing is your job. How does that feel to say out loud?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit embarrassing, actually. I'm proud of my slopes, but I know a computer can do a straight line better than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want to talk to about this at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My trainer, Mick. He's been on dozers for 30 years and he's honest. He'd tell me straight whether the face dozers are a smart move or not.

say: I'd tell my mum **people will adjust**, to calm her down.
At work I'd keep it **neutral**, because people get touchy.
think: Surveyors already use **drones and software**, so AI planning makes remote dozers easier.
A remote dozer could take over **simple pushing**, which is my job.
do: Finish my ticket and ask to move to the **bigger dozers** at the face.
Learn the **new planning apps** once a few others at the mine use them.
feel: **Uneasy**, with a path in sight that isn't fully clear.
S1.quote: I'm proud of my slopes, but I know a computer can do a straight line better than me.
fieldNote: Grace sees AI planning making **remote dozing** easier, not an immediate job loss.
She'd move to **harder dozer work**, a step up within the same job.
Her trusted adviser is **Mick**, her long-serving trainer.

steps.text: Ask trainer Mick about moving to the face dozers after her ticket
Learn the mine's new dump planning apps after a few colleagues do
Keep sending her mum 150 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one moves fast. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to be careful, and the company should tell us its plans. I wouldn't panic in public. I'd tell my mum it's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be scared. AGI plans the whole mine in 2028, then robots push the dirt by 2031. I'd be 32, no trade, three weeks of money and my mum leaning on me. There'd be a lot of miners looking for work in the same small town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving hard, right away, and drop the coast trips. I'd look at moving to the city where there are more kinds of work, maybe aged care or hospital work, where people still want a person. I'd ask the mine if they'd pay for a certificate in something before I go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Like I'm carrying my mum and me up the dump slope on foot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said aged care. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum's friend Sandra does it and she's never short of shifts. It's hard on your back, but people want a real person to help them. I'd rather do that than nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the money you send your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the worst part. If I move to the city, rent's higher, and I'd have to tell my mum I can only send 50 a month for a while. She'd understand, but I'd feel awful.

say: I'd say the **company should share** its plans with workers.
I'd tell my mum **it's fine**, and not panic in public.
think: By 2031 I'd be **32 with no trade** and three weeks of money.
Lots of miners would be **looking for work** in the same small town.
do: Start **saving hard** right away and drop the coast trips.
Look at **moving to the city** for aged care or hospital work.
Ask the mine to **pay for a certificate** before I leave.
feel: **Heavy**, like carrying my mum and me up a dump slope on foot.
S2.quote: If I move to the city, rent's higher, and I'd have to tell my mum I can only send 50 a month for a while.
fieldNote: The fast timeline brings Grace's **mum's support** into focus as the hardest cost.
She'd move toward **care work**, choosing jobs where people still want a person.
She keeps a **calm face** for her mother while privately expecting job loss.

steps.text: Drop the coast trips and save every spare dollar
Look for aged care or hospital work in the city
Ask the mine to pay for a care certificate before leaving
Plan a move to the city for more kinds of work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. A bit better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan, so let's plan. I'd tell people at work to get their tickets and certificates while the mine still pays for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gives me time to finish my dozer ticket, save something, and do a certificate on the side. AGI in 2031, robots in 2034. I'd be 35 by then, which isn't young, but it's not too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the ticket this year, then do a part-time aged care certificate online on my days off, once I see others doing it. I'd try to save three months. I'd keep the mine job as long as it's paying well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with a list. I like a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your four days off are your rest. Would you really give them up for study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of them. Two days of the four, maybe. I'd still need the coast to see Mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a moment you'd know it's time to leave the mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sign to leave the gold mine is when there's a dozer on the dumps with nobody in it. Not when the office gets AI, that's their problem.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to plan, so let's plan.
I'd tell workers to get **certificates** while the mine pays.
think: Five years lets me **finish my ticket**, save and study on the side.
At **35** I'm not young, but it's not too late.
do: Finish my **dozer ticket** this year and keep the mine job while it pays.
Do a **part-time aged care** certificate on two of my four days off.
Save up to **three months** of expenses.
feel: **Worried**, but with a list, and I like a list.
S3.quote: My sign to leave the gold mine is when there's a dozer on the dumps with nobody in it.
fieldNote: With five years Grace builds a **two-track plan**: keep the job, study care work.
Her **trigger** is a remote dozer on the dumps, not AI in the office.
She protects her **coast visits** to her mum even while studying.

steps.text: Finish the dozer ticket this year
Study an aged care certificate online on two days off each break
Save up to three months of expenses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I can work with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the sensible one. People should still prepare, but no need to panic. I'd say it at work and to my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still the same end, but ten years plus three is 2039. I'd have a dozer career, savings, maybe a partner. With ten years, I could choose when to leave the mine instead of being pushed. That makes a big difference to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working on the dozers and move up to the face. I'd save steadily. Around 2032 I'd start a care certificate or maybe a heavy plant mechanic course, depending on what's working for other people by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but the money is still thin, so I'd still be a little uneasy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe a partner. Would any of this change your family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. If I knew robots were coming in 2039, I'd want a partner with a different kind of job. Two miners in one house would be risky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your mum to know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm thinking ahead. She worries I'll get stuck the way she did at the laundromat. I'd want her to know I won't.

say: I'd call this the **sensible one**: prepare, but no need to panic.
I'd say that at work and **to my mum**.
think: By 2039 I'd have a **dozer career** and savings, so I could choose when to leave.
**Choosing** instead of being pushed makes a big difference.
do: Move up to the **face dozers** and save steadily.
Start a **care or plant mechanic** course around 2032, based on what works for others.
feel: **Calmer**, but still a little uneasy because money is thin.
S4.quote: With ten years, I could choose when to leave the mine instead of being pushed.
fieldNote: Ten years turns Grace's story into **choice**, not escape.
She thinks about **two incomes** in different fields, even in her partner choice.
Her **thin savings** keep a low hum of worry even here.

steps.text: Move up to the face dozers at the gold mine
Put a fixed amount into savings every pay
Start a care or plant mechanic course around 2032

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be out with no trade and my mum depending on me. What would help is the mine paying for a certificate before they let us go, and some help with moving costs for people who have to leave town.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about women on the mine. A lot of us came in the last five years. Women finally got into the mines, and it'd be a shame if the jobs disappeared right after.

headlineQuote: Women finally got into the mines, and it'd be a shame if the jobs disappeared right after.
portrait: Grace is a **trainee dozer operator** on the waste dumps at a gold mine, renting a room in a shared house.
She sends her mum **150 a month** and has about three weeks of savings.
She tries **new tech** once a friend has, and keeps a calm face in public.
In the fast AGI picture she'd move to the city for **care work**; with more time she'd plan it.
Her sign to leave is a **remote dozer** on the dumps.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd be out with no trade and her mum depending on her.
whatWouldHelp: The mine **paying for a certificate** before letting workers go.
Help with **moving costs** for people who must leave town.
